opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the nature of what we're asking models to do has changed. In the chat paradigm, the unit of value is a single response: the user asks something, the model answers, and post-training is mostly about making that one answer helpful, accurate, and well-formatted. Preference data, reward models, RLHF: all of that was built around judging a reply in isolation.

But the real value now is in getting things done, not answering questions. When a model writes code, debugs a repository, does research, or operates tools, the result emerges from a long trajectory of many steps. The model has to plan, act, observe feedback from an environment, recover from mistakes, and decide when it's finished. A single "good-looking" reply doesn't mean much. What matters is whether the task actually succeeded.

That shift changes almost everything in post-training. First, the reward signal moves from human preference on one turn toward outcome-based, often verifiable signals: did the tests pass, did the task complete. Second, the training data is no longer static prompt-response pairs. You need environments, interactive sandboxes where the model can act and get real feedback, and building those at scale becomes a core infrastructure problem. Third, the capabilities you're optimizing are different: long-horizon consistency, tool use, error correction, managing context over many steps. Chat-style training doesn't really exercise those, and in some cases it even works against them, because it rewards the model for sounding confident and complete in one shot rather than for exploring and verifying.

So to me it's not just a new application layer on top of the same models. If we believe the next stage of AI is models doing real work in the world, then post-training has to be redesigned around that goal. It means training in environments, on trajectories, against outcomes. Staying in the chat paradigm would mean optimizing for the wrong thing.

r001.rationale: The response explains training agents to use tools and succeed in interactive environments, but it does not identify reliability across different agent frameworks as a motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The simplest way I'd put it is that the chat paradigm optimizes for a single good answer, while the real world rewards getting things done. Those are very different objectives, and post-training is where you decide which one the model is actually being trained toward.

In the chat paradigm, the unit of work is one turn. The user asks, the model replies, and we grade that reply. RLHF, preference data, all the familiar machinery is built around "was this response good." That worked very well for a while, because a lot of value really is in one well-written answer. But it has a ceiling. The model learns to sound right, to be fluent and confident, rather than to be right in a way that holds up when you act on it. And the human raters can only check what they can see in that one turn.

The agent paradigm changes the unit of work from a response to a trajectory. The model has to plan, call tools, read what came back, notice when it was wrong, and recover. Most of the hard problems people want solved, whether it's fixing a bug across a codebase, doing a long research task, or handling a multi-step operation, look like this. You can't solve them in one shot, and you shouldn't pretend you can.

Once you frame it that way, several things follow for post-training. First, the reward has to come from outcomes, not from how the text looks. Did the tests pass, did the task actually get completed. That's a much more honest signal than a preference label, and it's much harder for the model to game by just being eloquent. Second, you need to train on long horizons, with real environments, where errors compound. A model that is 95 percent accurate per step is useless at step twenty unless it also knows how to check itself and backtrack. That self-correction behavior doesn't emerge from chat data. You have to put the model in situations where it fails and let it learn to recover.

Third, and I think this is underrated, the capability you're really trying to build is judgment about uncertainty. When to act, when to verify, when to stop and ask. A chat model has no cost for being wrong beyond a thumbs-down. An agent that runs a destructive command has real consequences. So post-training has to teach restraint and calibration, not just capability.

There's also a data reason. We've largely consumed the easy supply of high-quality human conversation data. Agent environments give you a way to generate signal at scale, because the environment itself can tell you whether you succeeded. That makes the whole loop much more scalable than paying people to rank answers.

So I don't see it as abandoning chat. Chat is a special case, one-step agent behavior. But if you keep optimizing for that special case, you train a model that's great at talking about doing things and mediocre at doing them. Moving post-training to the agent paradigm is just aligning the training objective with what we actually want the model to be useful for.

r001.rationale: The response argues for training agents to complete multi-step tasks reliably in environments, but it does not identify reliable performance across different agent frameworks as a motivation.

astra-6.text:
I think the core reason is that answering a question well and completing a task well are different capabilities. In a chat paradigm, we usually give the model a prompt and optimize the response. But when you ask it to do real work, producing a good response is only one part of the problem. It needs to decide what to do, take an action, observe the result, and adjust its next step.

That changes what post-training needs to teach. The model has to recognize when it lacks information, when to use a tool, and how to recover when an action fails. It also has to know when the task is actually finished. A response can sound very convincing while the underlying task remains incomplete.

So the training signal needs to extend beyond whether an individual answer looks good. We need to evaluate the whole trajectory: did the model achieve the goal, did it verify the outcome, and how much time and effort did it spend? That introduces harder problems, particularly credit assignment. If a task fails after twenty steps, which decision should we improve?

I wouldn’t say this means abandoning chat. Conversation is still an important way to communicate with the user. But the unit we optimize should move from a single response toward a completed task. That’s the fundamental shift.

r001.rationale: The response argues for optimizing completed tasks and full action trajectories, but does not identify reliability across different agent frameworks as a motivation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental reason is that the unit of work is changing. In the chat paradigm, we mostly train a model to produce a good response to a prompt. But in the agent paradigm, a response is only one step toward completing a task. The model has to decide what to do, use tools, interpret feedback, and keep going when something fails.

That changes what post-training needs to optimize. A response can look excellent in isolation and still lead the agent down the wrong path. Conversely, asking a clarifying question or running an extra check might look less impressive as a single answer, but be exactly what makes the task succeed. So we need to evaluate the whole trajectory and the final outcome, not just the quality of each message.

The training environment also becomes much more important. The model needs opportunities to act, observe consequences, and recover from mistakes. That creates challenges around long-horizon credit assignment and reliable rewards, but it also gives us a more meaningful learning signal: did the model actually accomplish what the user wanted?

For me, that is the key shift—from learning how to answer to learning how to get work done. Conversation remains important, but it becomes part of a broader ability to act.

r001.rationale: The response says agents must act, use tools, interpret feedback, and complete tasks, but does not identify reliability across different agent frameworks as a motivation for the shift.
